claims.claim: PyTorch 2.15: load_state_dict with strict=False returns _IncompatibleKeys(missing_keys, unexpected_keys); a prefixed checkpoint loads nothing and raises nothing; a size mismatch raises 'size mismatch for head.weight: copying a param with shape torch.Size([2, 8]) from checkpoint, the shape in current model is torch.Size([3, 8])' even with strict=False; strict=True reports 'Missing key(s) in state_dict'; torch.load refuses a pickled class by default with 'Weights only load failed'.
claims.source: Run on PyTorch 2.15.0 (PyPI wheel, CPU), November 2026.

claims.claim: B26 lab: with 60 labelled sequences, full fine-tuning from the pretrained encoder reached 0.992 mean validation accuracy over seeds 0 to 2, and training from scratch 0.759.

concept_html:
A pretrained model has learned from a large amount of unlabelled data. Fine-tuning starts from its weights and trains on your few labelled examples. In the B26 lab, an encoder pretrained on 20,000 unlabelled sequences reached 0.992 accuracy from 60 labels after full fine-tuning. The same model trained from random weights reached 0.759.

Weights travel as a state_dict: a dictionary from parameter names to tensors. In PyTorch 2.15:

torch.save(model.state_dict(), "encoder.pt")
state = torch.load("encoder.pt")      # weights_only=True by default since 2.6
result = model.load_state_dict(state, strict=False)
result.missing_keys, result.unexpected_keys

Three behaviours of load_state_dict matter when you fine-tune:

  • With the default strict=True, any missing or extra key raises RuntimeError.
  • With strict=False, it loads the keys that match and returns missing_keys and unexpected_keys. If every name carries an extra prefix such as model., nothing matches. Every key is reported, no weight loads, and no error is raised. Always read the result.
  • A key whose shape differs raises, even with strict=False. A checkpoint head with 2 outputs does not fit a new head with 3. Drop the old head's keys before loading.

The new head starts at random. Its keys appear in missing_keys, and that is expected. Any other missing key means the backbone did not load.

Then choose what trains. A frozen backbone with a new head, as in lesson B24-L5, is cheapest: call p.requires_grad_(False) on each backbone parameter. Full fine-tuning moves every weight, at a smaller learning rate. Lesson B26-L3 adds a third option, LoRA. Count what trains with sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad).

lines: import torch
from torch import nn
BACKBONE_PREFIX = "encoder."
def load_backbone(model: nn.Module, checkpoint: dict[str, torch.Tensor]) -> list[str]:
"""Copy the encoder weights from a pretraining checkpoint into a new model.
Args:
model: A model whose encoder sits under `encoder.`, with a new head.
checkpoint: A state_dict saved after pretraining.
Returns:
The model's keys the checkpoint did not fill, sorted: the new head.
Raises:
ValueError: If the checkpoint has no encoder keys, or the encoder did not load fully.
"""
backbone = {k: v for k, v in checkpoint.items() if k.startswith(BACKBONE_PREFIX)}
if not backbone:
raise ValueError("checkpoint has no keys starting with 'encoder.'")
result = model.load_state_dict(backbone, strict=False)
missing = [k for k in result.missing_keys if k.startswith(BACKBONE_PREFIX)]
if missing or result.unexpected_keys:
raise ValueError(f"encoder did not load: missing {missing}, unexpected {result.unexpected_keys}")
return sorted(result.missing_keys)

exercises.prompt_html:
Write compare_keys(model_keys, checkpoint_keys) -> tuple[list[str], list[str]], the check load_state_dict(strict=False) reports.

  • missing: model keys not in the checkpoint. unexpected: checkpoint keys not in the model.
  • Return both sorted, as (missing, unexpected).
exercises.solution:
def compare_keys(model_keys: list[str], checkpoint_keys: list[str]) -> tuple[list[str], list[str]]:
    """Keys a strict=False load would report.

    Args:
        model_keys: Parameter names of the model.
        checkpoint_keys: Names in the checkpoint.

    Returns:
        (missing, unexpected), each sorted.
    """
    model_set, checkpoint_set = set(model_keys), set(checkpoint_keys)
    return sorted(model_set - checkpoint_set), sorted(checkpoint_set - model_set)

exercises.prompt:
Checkpoints saved from a wrapper module carry a prefix such as `model.` on every key. Write `strip_prefix(state, prefix) -> dict`.

- Return a new dictionary with `prefix` removed from the start of every key, values unchanged.
- Raise `ValueError` if any key does not start with `prefix`, so a wrong prefix fails loudly.
exercises.prompt_html:
Checkpoints saved from a wrapper module carry a prefix such as model. on every key. Write strip_prefix(state, prefix) -> dict.

  • Return a new dictionary with prefix removed from the start of every key, values unchanged.
  • Raise ValueError if any key does not start with prefix, so a wrong prefix fails loudly.
exercises.solution:
def strip_prefix(state: dict[str, object], prefix: str) -> dict[str, object]:
    """Remove a wrapper prefix from every checkpoint key.

    Args:
        state: A state_dict, or any dictionary keyed by parameter name.
        prefix: The prefix every key must start with, such as "model.".

    Returns:
        A new dictionary with the prefix removed from each key.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If any key does not start with prefix.
    """
    wrong = [k for k in state if not k.startswith(prefix)]
    if wrong:
        raise ValueError(f"keys without prefix {prefix!r}: {wrong[:3]}")
    return {k.removeprefix(prefix): v for k, v in state.items()}

title: Transfer learning and loading pretrained weights
why_html: A team fine-tuned a pretrained text encoder on 500 coded survey answers and got accuracy no better than a model trained from scratch. The checkpoint had been saved from a wrapper module, so every key began with model.. The loading code used strict=False and ignored the result. No pretrained weight had loaded. Checking missing_keys would have shown the problem before the first epoch.
